newsitem.title: UK: Green lobby says UK budget comes up short.
newsitem.headline: Green lobby says UK budget comes up short.

text.p: Britain unveiled new taxes aimed at protecting the environment on Wednesday, but environmental campaigners called on the government to take more radical steps to prove its green credentials.

An increase on petrol duty announced by finance minister Gordon Brown in the new Labour government's first budget would do little to reduce carbon dioxide emissions unless the revenue was directed towards other green initiatives, they said.
Oil industry analysts said the changes would not prove tough enough to have any impact on Britain's traffic-clogged streets.

"We're disappointed. It's a missed opportunity to put the whole thing within the framework of an integrated transport strategy," said Simon Festing, transport campaigner at lobby group Friends of the Earth.
Brown raised excise duty on petrol by one percent to six percent over the rate of inflation, with the first annual increase of four pence a litre effective immediately.
"We want the majority of the money recycled into building up a decent, modern public transport system," said Charles Secrett, director of Friends of the Earth.
"We don't want a treasury tax raising exercise masquerading as a green tax," he added.
Environmental consultancy Transport 2000 said it welcomed the tax hike but was looking further initiatives.
"We now look for the integrated transport policy next year to make alternatives to driving easier and more attractive, and to review other subsidies to motoring," said director Stephen Joseph.
Britain wants to target a 20 percent cut on 1990 levels in carbon dioxide emissions by 2010 in order to combat global warming.
But higher petrol prices were unlikely to deter British motorists from filling up, industry analysts said.
"Customers are very conscious of price differences between brands and are very price aware, but total demand is all but inelastic to price," said Peter Regnier of Oil Price Assessments Ltd (OPAL).
"(The tax hike) is seen as a green ticket but its not going to have much affect on demand."
Taxes already make up more than three quarters of British pump prices, which stood at 59 pence for a litre of premium unleaded petrol on Friday, OPAL said.
But partly thanks to a fierce price war between oil companies and supermarket retailers, British motorists pay less than their counterparts in France, Italy and the Netherlands.
Environmental campaigners gave a muted welcome to a planned reduction in excise taxes to be introduced next year for buses and lorries that meet lower emissions standards.
But they said they were hoping that such a measure would also apply to private cars.
"We think it is more sensible to penalise the gas guzzling and most-polluting cars the most and reduce the tax on the most efficient cars," said Friends of the Earth's Secrett.
Brown also disappointed manufacturers of vehicles of designed to run on clean fuels such as compressed natural gas (CNG) and liquefied natural gas (LPG) by failing to cut duties on these fuels.
"It's disappointing that he hasn't been able to reduce excise duty on road fuel gases," said Tom Gorman of British Gas Natural Gas Vehicles.
Transport campaigners said that other measures that would encourage drivers to change their habits were also ignored.
In particular they were hoping for an end to mileage banding on tax relief for company car drivers which they say encourages extra driving.
"The system at the moment rewards people to do extra mileage," said Joseph of Transport 2000.
